The speech of the holy prophets is always unclear and filled with hidden meanings and divine mysteries, which they proclaimed beforehand. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, as it is written. It is necessary for those who want to understand these obscure and enigmatic theories to hasten to examine them with the eye of the mind, and to distinguish between the literal and spiritual interpretations, so that the benefit and clarification of the ideas may be evident to those who encounter them. I know that some have written about these things before and have made long speeches about them. But I think it is sufficient to provide a brief treatment, and not to give others an excuse for laziness, but rather to encourage them to speak and to follow the same path of interpretation. Since even if this happens, it would not be entirely bad, and through the agreement of the majority, the listeners may be led to the truth, I now persuade myself to undertake this task, believing that the labor and effort of good endeavors are more valuable than laziness, and that with God's guidance, it is possible to discover new and improved insights.

For it is written that 'your commandment is very broad.' The blessed Isaiah prophesied in the times of the kingdoms of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Let us recall the times of each and speak briefly. For from here, the word of prophecy is fitting and suitable for those who act at the right time. Uzziah, also called Ozias, was a pious man who advanced in glory and power, so that he dominated the surrounding nations, imposed taxes on many, and forced them to submit to his scepter, conquered cities, acquired others, and expanded the borders of Judah. Then he suffered something human. For, having been overcome by excessive luxury and the pride of his glory, he became somewhat foolish and, being dominated by the disease of haughtiness, rebelled against the divine law. He thought he should also crown himself with the diadems of divine priesthood. He attempted to enter the divine temple and offer incense to God himself, fulfilling the prescribed rites unlawfully. Because of this reason, he was immediately afflicted with leprosy and was most dishonored. For one who is afflicted with the disease of leprosy is unclean according to the law.

Then Joatham, a God-loving man, but not removing the high places, succeeds Ozias' kingdom, and the Israelites still sacrifice on the works of their own hands, on mountains and hills, under trees, as Hosea says, that shade is good; after Joatham's death, Ahaz, a detestable and God-hating man, full of wickedness, succeeds, closing the divine temple and not allowing the lawful sacrifices, and forbidding the festivals of the Jews, and setting up altars everywhere in Jerusalem to worship the handmade idols and the heavenly army; Ahaz also burned his own children as a sacrifice to the unclean demons, and no kind of impiety was unfamiliar to him; then Hezekiah, a pious and God-loving man, a leader of righteousness and a zealous seeker of good, and a worker of divine wills, reigns, and he commands to stop all the transgressions of Ahaz, and to open the doors of the temple, and to offer sacrifices and libations to God, and to perform the lawful priestly services, and he also renews the law of the Passover after a long time

He commanded temples and altars and handmade things to cease, and he knew false prophets and the crowds of enchanters, and he was a good man in the eyes of God, and since the times of the recently mentioned kingdoms, sometimes God was provoked to anger at Israel's idolatry, and sometimes he was softened towards mildness through the ruler's gentleness, and thus the word of prophecy is mixed, and most of the time it makes threats as if Israel is disobedient, but it also brings in a word of promise for good things, and it remembers everywhere the redemption through Christ, and says that at times Israel will be sent away from God's intimacy, but the multitude of the nations will be justified through faith in Christ, so I think Isaiah the prophet is crowned well, not only with the gift of prophecy, but also with apostolic sufferings, for he is both a prophet and an apostle at the same time, and he has not been deprived of the brightness of the evangelical preachings
pass_b_english: The prophets' words are shrouded in mystery, filled with hidden meanings and divine secrets that they proclaimed beforehand. To grasp these obscure and enigmatic theories, one must hasten to examine them with the eye of the mind, distinguishing between the literal and spiritual interpretations.

For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, as it is written. Some have written about these things before, making long speeches, but I believe a brief treatment is sufficient. I do not want to give others an excuse for laziness, but rather to encourage them to speak and follow the same path of interpretation. Even if this effort is not entirely new, it can still lead listeners to the truth, and with God's guidance, it is possible to discover new insights.

The commandment of God is very broad, as it is written. The prophet Isaiah spoke during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Let us consider the times of each of these kings and speak briefly about them. From this point on, the word of prophecy is fitting and suitable for those who act at the right time. Uzziah, also known as Ozias, was a pious man who advanced in glory and power, dominating the surrounding nations and imposing taxes on many. He conquered cities, acquired others, and expanded the borders of Judah.

However, Uzziah's success eventually led to his downfall. He became overcome with excessive luxury and the pride of his glory, which made him foolish and haughty. As a result, he rebelled against the divine law and attempted to enter the divine temple to offer incense to God himself, fulfilling the prescribed rites unlawfully. This act of hubris led to his immediate affliction with leprosy, making him most dishonored. According to the law, one who is afflicted with leprosy is unclean.

After Ozias, his descendant Joatham, a God-loving man, though not one to remove the high places, took over the kingdom. The Israelites continued to sacrifice on the works of their own hands, on mountains and hills, under trees, as Hosea says, that shade is good. Following Joatham's death, Ahaz, a detestable and God-hating man, full of wickedness, succeeded him.

Ahaz closed the divine temple, forbidding the lawful sacrifices, and prohibited the festivals of the Jews. He set up altars everywhere in Jerusalem to worship the handmade idols and the heavenly army. Ahaz even burned his own children as a sacrifice to the unclean demons, and no kind of impiety was unfamiliar to him. Then, Hezekiah, a pious and God-loving man, a leader of righteousness and a zealous seeker of good, and a worker of divine wills, reigns. He commands to stop all the transgressions of Ahaz, to open the doors of the temple, and to offer sacrifices and libations to God, performing the lawful priestly services. He also renews the law of the Passover after a long time.

The prophet commanded that temples, altars, and handmade objects cease to be used, and he was aware of false prophets and the crowds of enchanters. He was a good man in the eyes of God. In the times of the kingdoms that have recently been mentioned, God was sometimes provoked to anger at Israel's idolatry, and at other times he was softened towards mildness through the ruler's gentleness.

The word of prophecy is mixed, and most of the time it makes threats as if Israel is disobedient, but it also brings in a word of promise for good things. Everywhere, it remembers the redemption through Christ, saying that at times Israel will be sent away from God's intimacy, but the multitude of the nations will be justified through faith in Christ. I think that Isaiah the prophet is crowned well, not only with the gift of prophecy, but also with apostolic sufferings, for he is both a prophet and an apostle at the same time, and he has not been deprived of the brightness of the evangelical preachings. He is a man who has been good in the eyes of God, and his prophetic word has been mixed with the promise of redemption through Christ.
